problems.description: _send_connection swallows every exception with a bare 'except Exception: pass', masking real send failures behind a comment; error telemetry is lost and this will compound across later story sessions.
start() reaches into private aiohttp internals (_health_site._server.sockets) to discover the ephemeral port, coupling NotificationServer to library internals.
threading.RLock in ClientRegistry is unnecessary in a single-event-loop context (asyncio already serializes handlers); adds a threading dependency and a false concurrency model.

Grounded in measurement: convention score 0.82 with 4 violations — app.py and test_notification_server.py classes not PascalCase; test_notification_server.py and transport.py module constants not UPPER_CASE.
Tests cover broadcast/health/id assignment but not direct messages, invalid-payload error paths, or disconnect cleanup (client registry removal on close).

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: ClientRegistry (state) vs NotificationServer (orchestration), each single-purpose and easily testable.
Strong convention fit in visible code: snake_case functions, PascalCase classes, and full type hints on all public signatures, matching AGENTS.md conventions.
Correct async lifecycle management — start/stop pair with explicit resource cleanup and ephemeral-port support for tests.
Defensive broadcast pattern: snapshot() avoids mutating the registry during iteration.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid greenfield baseline — well-factored async server with good convention fit (0.82, matching the visible code) — but the error-swallowing in _send_connection and private-attribute port discovery are debt to pay down; note the measurement's app.py/transport.py violations fall in the truncated part of the diff so they could not be verified directly.

problems.description: Measured convention score 0.82 with 4 violations, but all flagged violations (PascalCase classes in app.py and test_notification_server.py, UPPER_CASE constants in test_notification_server.py and transport.py) are in pre-existing files/lines, not introduced by this diff.

_broadcast_channel and channel_snapshot rebuild and sort the subscription snapshot on every message, copying all subscriber sets per send rather than holding a reference — O(channels) copy per broadcast.
Routing logic applies channel broadcast before the 'direct' branch, so any message type (including 'direct') carrying a 'channel' payload silently routes to the channel instead of its declared type.

strengths: Thread-safe subscription state encapsulated in ClientRegistry with proper RLock usage and cleanup of empty channels
Subscriptions are automatically pruned when a client disconnects via remove(), preventing stale membership leaks
Input validation (_valid_channel) rejects empty/non-string channel names before registration
Comprehensive tests cover subscribe/broadcast isolation, unsubscribe, empty-channel listing, and multi-channel scenarios
New HTTP endpoints (_channels, _channel_subscribers) follow the existing aiohttp handler and json_response conventions
Consistent use of asyncio.gather for fan-out delivery, matching the existing _broadcast pattern
commit_reviews.summary: A well-factored, pattern-conforming channel subscription feature that extends the existing ClientRegistry/aiohttp architecture cleanly, with all measured convention violations being pre-existing.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity increased by +46 (SonarQube delta), concentrated in the connection-handling path that now parses client IDs from request paths; the handler is growing large and would benefit from extraction into focused helpers.

MessageStore opens a fresh sqlite3 connection on every add/list call, and add() runs synchronously on the event loop from the publish path; a shared connection (or aio-sqlite/async wrapper) would avoid per-op connect overhead and event-loop blocking.

Introduces the redis package (async API) without evidence it is declared in project dependencies; RedisBackbone is gated on env vars so it degrades gracefully, but the import makes `redis` a hard dependency of the module.
The new /messages history endpoint is unauthenticated and pagination params are only range-validated, not rate-limited; acceptable for a localhost service but worth documenting.

The measured convention score of 0.82 is pulled down by PascalCase/constant-case violations in app.py, test_notification_server.py, and transport.py — none of which are touched by this commit; the commit's own new code (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE REDIS_CHANNEL) is conformant.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: RedisBackbone (transport/durable subscription state), MessageStore (persistence), NotificationServer (orchestration), mirroring the existing ClientRegistry pattern.
Graceful degradation — Redis failure is caught in start() and the server continues serving without a backbone.
Backward-compatible API change: ClientRegistry.add() keeps its signature via an optional client_id parameter.
Proper async lifecycle: pubsub listener task is cancelled and awaited in close(); HTTP runner and backbone cleanup are symmetric.
Parameterized SQL and strict validation of limit/offset on the new /messages endpoint; blocking sqlite reads are offloaded with asyncio.to_thread.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured integration commit that adds a Redis pub/sub backbone and SQLite message history with graceful fallback and clean lifecycle handling, at the cost of notable cognitive complexity and minor connection-management inefficiencies.

problems.description: ClientRegistry connection type downgraded from ServerConnection to Any across add/get/snapshot, eliminating static type safety on the registry surface — conflicts with the repo's 'type hints on public signatures' convention.

SonarQube reports +7 smells and +33 cognitive complexity: the transport abstraction splits connection lifecycle across _transport_connect/_transport_ready/_transport_disconnect, spreading logic that was previously linear in _handle_connection.
+4.5% duplication introduced by the new transport layer, indicating shared send/broadcast paths were not fully consolidated.
New transport.py module-level constants are not UPPER_CASE (measured convention violation).

The exception-swallowing send guard in _send_connection (connection closes between snapshot and send) was removed; correctness now depends on transport.send_message/broadcast swallowing closed-connection errors.

strengths: Pluggable BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport decouples routing from the websockets library, enabling alternative transports and testability.
Env-driven transport selection (TRANSPORT) with constructor injection and validation for unknown transports.
Symmetric start/stop lifecycle and client_id-based addressing (connect/ready/disconnect) cleanly separate registry bookkeeping from transport I/O.
Broadcast/send logic consolidated behind the transport interface, removing per-call gather boilerplate from the server.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-motivated transport-abstraction refactor that improves modularity and testability, offset by a type-safety downgrade to Any and a rise in complexity/duplication.

problems.description: Two parallel rate-limiting mechanisms added in the same commit — RedisBackbone.allow_message (INCR/EXPIRE) and NotificationServer._rate_windows (in-memory window). No clear seam or authority; one path is likely dead code and the two can diverge in behavior under load.
_rate_windows dict has no eviction policy for stale client_ids; it grows unboundedly across sessions, a memory leak under many concurrent clients.

History/TTL filtering compares ISO timestamps as strings (timestamp > ? / < ?); ordering only holds if every stored timestamp shares an exact format, and the since-parser normalizes Z→+00:00 while stored rows may keep 'Z', breaking lexicographic comparison across mixed formats.
RATE_LIMIT and MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS are each parsed via an identical duplicated try/except/raise block; a small config helper would remove the duplication.
No tests for the new rate-limit, history, or TTL-cleanup paths appear in the diff (truncated — verify); these cross-cutting behaviors are untested surface.

strengths: list_history/_history mirror the existing _messages handler conventions (query validation, limit bounds 1..1000, asyncio.to_thread) — good pattern reuse.
Pagination via limit+1 with has_more is a clean, standard approach.
threading.RLock on MessageStore access is consistent with the to_thread usage and closes a real concurrency gap.
Cleanup task cancellation in stop() with asyncio.gather(return_exceptions=True) and reset is correct teardown.
Positive-integer validation with explicit error messages for both new env vars.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, convention-consistent feature commit that adds real value (history endpoint, TTL cleanup, concurrency lock) but introduces technical debt via duplicate rate-limiting implementations and an unbounded in-memory rate window.

compounding_issues: Binary build artifacts (__pycache__/*.pyc, messages.db) were committed in sessions 2, 3, and 5, adding repo noise that was never cleaned
Session 3's Redis integration shipped a client-API bug (aclose vs close) that failed a test mid-session and required immediate patching, indicating a rushed integration
Session 5 introduced dual, potentially-divergent rate-limiting code paths (Redis INCR vs an in-process sliding window fallback) that can drift in behavior
The seed codebase (app.py todo API) was discarded entirely in session 1; the story went greenfield and never leveraged or removed the seed's notification stub
key_decisions: Session 1: build on aiohttp + asyncio websockets with a thread-safe ClientRegistry and clean start/stop lifecycle, keeping the whole server in a single file
Session 2: extend the message protocol with subscribe/unsubscribe channel semantics and expose /channels REST introspection endpoints
Session 3: adopt a RedisBackbone pub/sub layer for cross-instance fan-out with durable subscription state, plus a SQLite MessageStore for message persistence
Session 4: extract a BaseTransport ABC / WebSocketTransport into transport.py, decoupling routing from the socket layer and making the transport pluggable
Session 5: add operational hardening — Redis-based rate limiting, message TTL retention cleanup, SQLite thread synchronization, and env-driven configuration
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the 5 sessions: test count grew 3 -> 5 -> 7 -> 7 -> 9 with all tests green at every commit. Session 1 laid a clean single-file foundation, sessions 2 and 3 stacked features rapidly (channels, persistence, Redis fan-out) with a brief mid-session Redis API stumble, session 4 was a genuine architectural refactor introducing a pluggable transport abstraction without regressing tests, and session 5 rounded out the arc with operational concerns (rate limiting, message retention, thread safety). Minor hygiene slips — committing pyc/db artifacts and leaving a dead seed app — persisted, but architectural structure and test coverage consistently trended upward.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, steadily-improving story in which a greenfield notification server matured from a single-file WebSocket demo through channel routing, Redis/SQLite distribution, a transport-layer refactor, and operational hardening, with only minor hygiene and dual-implementation warts.
